::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Is this set open or closed](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1149103/is-this-set-open-or-closed), asked by [matthew](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/215613/matthew) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2015-02-15; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Is $(-1,0]\cup[0,1)$ open or closed, both or neither (relative to R)?
>
> This set doesn't contain the limit point $1$, so it's not closed. But how can I determine whether it's open or not? The complement is $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$, but I can't seem to figure out whether it's closed or not. I would say it's closed because it contains every point, so that would make $(-1,0]\cup[0,1)$ an open set, but the infinity thing kinda sets me off.
:::

I don't know how the topology of $\mathbb{R}$ is defined in your course, but in a metric space (of which $\mathbb{R}$ is an example), a set is open if for each point of the set there is a ball of finite radius around the point contained within the set.

So open intervals $(a,b)$ in $\mathbb{R}$ are open, because for any $x_0 \in (a,b)$, the ball of radius $\min\left(\frac{x_0-a}{2},\frac{b-x_0}{2}\right)$ is contained in $(a,b)$ (draw a picture and you'll see what this means).

Then you just have to realize that $(-1,0]\cup[0,1)$ is the same set as $(-1,1)$.
